Part I

MoshiVis

Adding vision to a frozen real-time speech model

CVPR 2026 arxiv:2503.15633

Moshi: The backbone

  • ~7B parameter speech LM
  • Operates at 12.5 Hz (Mimi codec)
  • Hard constraint: <80 ms/step
  • Speaks and listens simultaneously

→ How to integrate vision inputs in Moshi in real-time?

MoshiVis: Gated cross-attention

Image tokens as keys/values — never enter KV cache:

CA(x | y) = MHA(x | y1…N)

Combined with SA via a learnable gate:

out = SA(x) + g(x) · CA(x, img)
  • Gate g(x) learns to switch off vision — zero supervision
  • g → 0 recovers base Moshi exactly

Speechless + speech mixed training

  • Mix paudio% speech + (1−paudio)% text-only image data
  • Knowledge transfers across modalities
  • paudio = 25% is sufficient — 4× data savings

Audio eval accuracy vs. paudio

Listening test: paudio = 5% vs. 100%

Unprompted — model speaks freely about the image, no text prompt

Trained with paudio = 5%

Trained with paudio = 25%

Reference: paudio = 100%

Gating: Context switching

  • Without gate: MMLU drops 5–10% after an image prefix
  • With gate: <3% degradation
  • Learned automatically — zero supervision

Part II

MoshiVis
meets Video

Frame swapping at inference — and what comes next

Extending to video: Swap frames in CA

CA(xt | framet)   ∀t
  • Tracks scene changes, answers frame-specific questions
  • Not trained for video — static images only during training
  • No temporal consistency

Alternative: Chunk-based video (e.g. MiniCPM-V)

Chunk video into 1s segments, insert tokens per chunk:

  • Delay: must wait for the full chunk before responding
  • KV cache accumulates all past chunks — scales poorly

Why isn't cross-attention more widely used for video?

Prior work (mPLUG-Owl3, StreamChat) reported CA consistently underperforming insertion. Architectural, or training artefact?

→ Systematic analysis: CASA

Part III

CASA

A systematic comparison of cross-attention vs. token insertion

Pre-print arxiv:2512.19535

Token insertion vs. cross-attention: Five differences

Token insertion (SA)
KV grows with every frame

Cross-attention (CA)
Images never in KV cache

D1→D5 progressively recovers insertion from CA:

  • D1 Extra parameters
  • D2 Joint text-image attention + pos. emb.
  • D3 Additional layers
  • D4 Image token updates
  • D5 Multi-image KV history

CA enables longer videos without OOM

Walltime vs. frames. Token Isnertion hits OOM early even with token compression (Q-Former); CA scales linearly.

  • Q-Former (≥64 queries) hits OOM before 250 frames
  • CA scales to 750+ frames on the same budget
  • CA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL 3B matches 7B LiveCC models on LiveSports3K

Part IV

What's Next

Toward a strong audio-vision omni backbone — three open problems

Three open problems

1 · Data

No dense visual grounding in existing video dialogue data.

→ Synthetic: VLM captions + LLM dialogue + TTS

2 · Architecture

CA sees one window — no compressed history.

→ Gist tokens · SSMs · KV compression

CA(xt | framet, gistt-1)

3 · Vision Encoding

CLIP is static — no motion or temporal dynamics.

→ Codec encoder: Motion & scene-change as natural inductive bias

Summary

Part I · MoshiVis
  • Gated cross-attention on a frozen speech LM (206M trainable params)
  • Learned gate suppresses vision without explicit supervision
  • Mixed speechless training: paudio = 25% sufficient; +7 ms/step overhead, stays within real-time constraint
Part II · Video
  • Frame swapping in CA keys/values enables streaming video at inference
  • No additional training required on video data
  • In contrast, chunk-based insertion accumulates in KV cache — memory grows linearly with duration
Part III · CASA
  • Under a fair modern pipeline, CA matches prior SA SotA on most VLM benchmarks
  • 6.1 GB inference memory vs. 27.1 GB for token insertion at 60 frames
  • CA models scales to 750+ frames; Token insertion (even with token merging) OOMs before 250
Open directions
  • Synthetic audio-visual dialogue data (VLM + LLM + TTS pipeline)
  • Compressed visual history for long-form video (gist tokens, SSMs)
  • Codec-based vision encoder with temporal inductive biases

Takeaway: cross-attention is memory-constant w.r.t. visual context, streaming-compatible, and — under a controlled training setup — competitive with token insertion across standard benchmarks.
